summary:
Swell is a web app that turns twenty years of NASA sea level data into sound, built first for people who are blind or have low vision. Using JPL’s MEaSUREs sea surface height maps, we took one map each May from 1999 to 2018 and gave every spot a voice. Higher seas play higher notes, west to east moves from your left ear to your right, and a steady tone marks normal so listeners always know where they stand. Users can play the whole story in ten seconds, drag a finger across the map to hear any spot, or pick a coastal place like Wilmington, North Carolina and hear its twenty years.

The Earth Information Jukebox challenge asks teams to make Earth data something you can hear. Almost all climate data is shared as maps and charts, which leaves millions of people out. Swell lets them hear the trend for themselves. It runs in any browser on phones and laptops with no install or account, collects nothing about the user, and follows accessibility guidance on contrast, readable fonts, spacing and screen reader support. Everyone can use it, but it was designed around the people who are usually left out.
details:
What it does and how it works

Swell turns twenty years of NASA sea level data into sound. We used JPL’s MEaSUREs Gridded Sea Surface Height Anomalies (version 2205) and took one global map each May from 1999 to 2018. Our Python pipeline reads each map’s colors back into sea level values and saves them with the app.

In the browser, every spot on the map becomes a note:

  • Higher seas play higher notes.
  • West to east moves from your left ear to your right.
  • Different instruments mark how far above or below normal a spot is.
  • A steady reference tone always marks “normal,” so you can tell where you stand without seeing anything.

You can listen in three ways:

  • Play all twenty years as one piece.
  • Drag a finger across the map, or use the arrow keys, to hear any spot.
  • Pick one of 31 coastal places, like Wilmington, North Carolina, and hear its twenty years.

The app also reads each year out loud in plain words.

Benefits

Almost all climate data is shared as maps and charts. Swell gives people who are blind or have low vision a way to experience that data for themselves, instead of having someone describe a picture. It runs in any web browser on phones and laptops. There’s nothing to install, no account, and nothing collected about the user, including location.

Intended impact

We want a blind student to be able to follow sea level rise in the same science class as everyone else, and teachers, museums and families to be able to use it with no setup. Hearing the notes climb year after year also makes the trend stick for sighted listeners.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks) for the app. Python for the data pipeline and local server.
  • Browser features: Web Audio API for all sound, made live on the device. Web Speech API for read aloud, using the device’s own voice. Canvas for the map.
  • Python libraries: NumPy, Pillow, FastAPI and Uvicorn. earthaccess and xarray for downloading and reading NASA data.
  • Fonts: Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (made with the Braille Institute for low vision readers), OpenDyslexic, and Zilla Slab and Alfa Slab One for headings.
  • Testing: Playwright for automated browser tests and axe for accessibility scans, plus real iPhones and laptops.
  • Hosting and teamwork: GitHub for version control and Cloudflare Workers for hosting.

What makes it creative

Most data sonifications are recordings you just press play on. Swell is interactive. You explore the map with your finger and hear exactly where the sea has risen most. The reference tone gives listeners a fixed point to compare against, much like a horizon line on a chart. The whole design follows a nautical chart theme, with anchors, compasses and curling waves, while the plain high contrast themes switch the decoration off.

What we considered

  • Accessibility first: WCAG contrast and text spacing rules, nine color themes including high contrast and dyslexia friendly backgrounds, three text sizes, screen reader announcements, keyboard shortcuts, reduced motion and a large cursor. Automated scans found zero WCAG errors on all nine themes.
  • Phones first: WebAIM’s survey found 91.3% of screen reader users use one on a phone. We fixed phone specific problems like iPhone sound rules and memory limits.
  • Honest data: comparing the same month each year so the seasons don’t muddy the trend.
  • Privacy and simplicity: no accounts, no tracking, no setup.
